Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The profile otherwise reflects fear, vigilance, avoidance of proximity/anger cues, and beliefs that others may harm her. In that context, endorsing risky or self-endangering behavior is hard to reconcile clinically, especially with no Maladaptive Strategies items or other disinhibition/externalising content to support it.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, a global appraisal that 'you can never know who will harm you' is possible but sits somewhat awkwardly beside highly specific interpersonal triggers (physical proximity, others' anger) and trauma-linked memory content. It implies diffuse unpredictability of all potential perpetrators rather than the more coherent expected pattern of threat from close others or angry interpersonal situations.

vignette:
Ama

Ama was seventy-seven when she finally named what had happened to her at fifty-one. For twenty-six years she had carried the injury as something private, something she had learned to work around the way one works around a chronic pain-by adjusting posture, by avoiding certain movements, by pretending the damage was not there. It was only when her daughter, now a physician, had gently suggested that her mother's vigilance at night, her way of checking the locks three times before bed and sleeping with her hand on a phone, might be connected to something that needed attention, that Ama had begun to acknowledge the shape of what her then-husband had done to her.

The beating had occurred on an ordinary Tuesday evening in their home in Atlanta. He had come home angry-she could not now recall what had triggered it, though she had spent decades trying to piece together that missing part, as if understanding the cause might retroactively make sense of the violence. What remained vivid was fragmented: his voice rising, her own body moving backward through the kitchen, the moment when his hand connected with her face and she felt something inside her skull shift. After that, the memory became a series of photographs with gaps between them. She remembered blood on her hands-his or hers, she was no longer certain-and a ringing in her ears. She remembered the floor, and then nothing, and then the hospital, and then the careful lie she had constructed for the emergency room doctor about a fall.

She had left him six months later, but the fear had never left. What frightened her most was not the possibility that he would find her now, decades later, a woman in her late seventies with a career in local politics and a different life in a different city. What frightened her was that she no longer fully trusted her own mind to hold the story intact. Whenever she tried to remember the complete sequence of events, something in her would rebel. She would begin to recall his expression, the words he had said, and then a pressure would build in her chest and she would push the memory away, as if her own mind were protecting her from something she could not bear to know. The gaps remained. She had come to believe that this fragmentation was permanent damage, that some part of her had been irreversibly broken that night and would never be whole again.

The triggers were everywhere, though she had become expert at managing them. When a colleague in the city council chamber raised his voice during a heated debate about zoning ordinances-his tone perfectly reasonable, his anger measured and professional-Ama found her breathing shallow, her body tense. She would excuse herself, citing a need to check on something in her office, and would sit alone for ten minutes, reminding herself that this man was not him, that anger itself was not violence. But the distinction had become difficult to maintain. Any expression of anger, even when she knew intellectually it posed no threat, sent a signal through her body that danger was near.

Proximity was worse. When someone stood too close to her at a community event or a political fundraiser, she would feel her shoulders rise, her jaw tighten. She had developed the habit of positioning herself near doorways, of keeping her back to a wall. At night, the vigilance intensified. She lay awake, listening to the sounds of her house, checking the locks repeatedly even though she had already checked them. Her husband, Marcus, had learned not to approach her suddenly in the darkness; more than once she had startled so violently at his touch that she had nearly struck him.

The guilt was perhaps the most isolating aspect. When she allowed herself to remember-when the fragments came together briefly before she could push them away-she felt a crushing sense of shame, as if she had somehow caused the violence, as if her failure to understand what had angered him had invited the blow. She had never told Marcus the full story. She had told him there had been an abusive relationship, that it had ended, that it had left its mark. But the specifics, the blood, the gaps in her memory, the way she sometimes could not trust her own recollection of what had happened-these she kept to herself.

She had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that the violence she had experienced was not exceptional but rather the true nature of intimate relationships, revealed. She had built a career, maintained a marriage, raised children, and done all of it while operating from the conviction that she had been permanently altered, that whatever capacity she had once possessed for genuine feeling, for openness, for the kind of trust that allows a person to truly rest, had been destroyed that Tuesday evening and would never return. It was only when she could no longer hide the nighttime vigilance, when her startle response had become so pronounced that she had jumped at a colleague's greeting and caused a small scene at a public event, that she had finally agreed to seek help. She was afraid that speaking about it would make it more real, but she was also afraid that remaining silent would mean living the rest of her life as a prisoner of fragments and fear.
